scope: grade 6 NY-6.NS.4 to NS.8 and NY-6.G.3

g6-2023-013.quote: What is the least common multiple of 6 and 9?
g6-2023-013.why: The item asks for the least common multiple of 9 and 12 with no context at all. Lesson 17's Cool-down asks exactly that bare question about 6 and 9 and requires the reasoning shown, so it is where the curriculum tests this skill in the item's own form.

g6-2024-043.quote: In your own words, what is the greatest common factor of two whole numbers?
g6-2024-043.why: The item hands students a wrong claim (4 is the GCF of 24 and 40 because both are multiples of 4) and asks them to judge it, which turns on the difference between a common factor and the greatest one. Lesson 16's Cool-down asks for a GCF with reasoning and then asks students to define the greatest common factor in their own words, which is precisely the distinction the claim gets wrong.

g6-2025-039.quote: What is the greatest common factor of 24 and 64?
g6-2025-039.why: The item is a bare 'what is the greatest common factor of 72 and 96' with a written answer. Lesson 16's Cool-down asks the same bare question about 24 and 64 and is the assessment point for the skill.

g6-2026-017.lessonTitle: Using Common Multiples and Common Factors
g6-2026-017.quote: Find the smallest number of plates and cups that meets her requirement.
g6-2026-017.why: The item asks after how many days two activities recurring every 6 and every 8 days coincide again (answer 24). Lesson 18's first activity opens with cups sold in packs of 8 and plates in packs of 6 and asks for the smallest number that works, which is the same least-common-multiple-of-6-and-8 question with the same answer. The optional second activity in the same lesson ('Soccer', a game every 3rd and every 4th day) matches the item's every-N-days framing even more closely, but it is optional work.

g6-2025-031.lessonTitle: Using Negative Numbers to Make Sense of Contexts
g6-2025-031.quote: For which items did the event planner receive money?
g6-2025-031.why: The item asks which pair of integers represents a $65 deposit and a $20 withdrawal, i.e. that money in is positive and money out is negative. Lesson 5's Cool-down gives a table where money received is positive and money spent is negative and asks students to sort the two directions apart. The curriculum asks students to interpret signs already supplied rather than to choose the signs themselves; the closest place students assign the sign is Lesson 2's practice problem 4 ('Represent each of these temperatures ... with a positive or negative number'), which is not an activity.

g6-2026-002.quote: describe the elevation of Death Valley, CA in relation to sea level
g6-2026-002.why: The item shows three city elevations on a number line at -5, -2 and 2 and asks which statement about above or below sea level is true. Lesson 1's second activity gives a table of city elevations including negative ones and asks students to describe each in relation to sea level, which is the same reading of sign as direction from zero.

g6-2024-018.quote: What is the opposite of the opposite of -3.2?
g6-2024-018.why: The item asks which expression represents the opposite of -2 1/2, with the key being the nested negation -(-2 1/2). Lesson 2's Cool-down is the only place in the unit that asks for the opposite of the opposite of a negative number. Worth knowing: the curriculum always says 'the opposite of' in words and never writes the -(-a) notation in an activity or practice problem, which fits this item's very low p-value of 0.28.

g6-2026-008.quote: Which number is the same distance away from 0 as is the number -7?
g6-2026-008.why: The item asks which of four plotted points is the opposite of 4 1/2, i.e. the point the same distance from 0 on the other side. Lesson 2's folding activity defines opposites as two numbers the same distance from 0 and asks students to find the partner of a given number on the number line.

g6-2024-026.quote: connect opposite signs in coordinates to reflections across one or both axes
g6-2024-026.why: The item asks for the reflection of (-4, 6) over the x-axis. Lesson 14's first activity is the one place the curriculum pairs points whose coordinates differ by sign and asks how far each is from each axis and on which side, which is exactly the rule that flips the y-coordinate.

g6-2023-002.activity: A Point on the Number Line
g6-2023-002.quote: Which of the following numbers could be represented by point B?
g6-2023-002.why: The item asks which of four plotted points is -1 1/3, so students must judge which two integers the value falls between. Lesson 2's Warm-up asks the same matching question in the other direction and its narrative says its purpose is to prime students to locate negative fractions by discerning which two numbers a value is between.

g6-2025-003.quote: Write the coordinates of each labeled point.
g6-2025-003.why: The item asks which of four plotted points is at (-2, 3), all four in different quadrants. Lesson 11's first activity is where the plane is extended to four quadrants and students both read coordinates off labeled points and plot a point at (-2, 5).

g6-2024-029.quote: larger numbers are to the right on a horizontal number line
g6-2024-029.why: The item supplies the true inequality -9/20 > -21/24 and asks students to say where the two numbers sit relative to each other and to 0 on a number line. Lesson 3's first activity establishes that larger numbers are to the right and smaller to the left, and its Jada question ('I know that 14 is less than 21, so -14 is also less than -21') is the exact misconception the item's distractors trade on. The companion activity 'Rational Numbers on a Number Line' (p. 51) is the non-assessed runner-up.

g6-2023-038.quote: Use the symbol < or > to compare the elevations
g6-2023-038.why: The item asks students to write a statement using an inequality symbol to compare -27 F and -35 F. Lesson 3's Cool-down asks for exactly that, a symbol comparison written between two signed elevations placed on a number line.

g6-2026-039.quote: Use the symbol < or > to compare the elevations of Death Valley and Westmorland.
g6-2026-039.why: The item asks for a numerical statement with >, < or = comparing -5 F and -9 F, both negative. The Cool-down's third question compares -282 and -157 feet, the both-negative case, which is where the ordering of negatives actually has to be reasoned about rather than read off.

g6-2023-017.quote: Which temperature is closer to the freezing point: -6 °C or 3 °C?
g6-2023-017.why: The item gives four elevations (83, -122, 456, -17 feet) and asks which is closest to sea level, which is a comparison of absolute values across signs. Lesson 6's second activity asks which of a negative and a positive temperature is closer to the reference point and then names that as the smaller absolute value, and its second half does the same with elevations above and below sea level.

g6-2026-020.lessonTitle: Comparing Numbers and Distance from Zero
g6-2026-020.quote: Mark each statement as true or false, and explain your reasoning.
g6-2026-020.why: The item asks which statement about -15 and -5 is true, and each choice pairs an order comparison with an absolute-value comparison, so students must hold the two apart. Lesson 7's Cool-down does exactly that: its first two statements order -5 against 3 and its last two compare the absolute value of -5 against 3. The absolute-value bars are lost from the extracted text (all four statements read as '-5 < 3' or '-5 > 3'), but the guide's own sample response restores them by reasoning that the absolute value of -5 is 5, and 5 > 3.

g6-2024-004.activity: Finding Distances in a Coordinate Plane
g6-2024-004.quote: Find the distance between each pair of points.
g6-2024-004.why: The item gives (-7, -8) and (-7, 4) as text with no picture and asks for the distance, a vertical span crossing the x-axis. Lesson 14's second activity is where students develop strategies for horizontal and vertical distances, including pairs that cross an axis. Note the curriculum always supplies the grid; the item does not.

g6-2024-045.quote: What is the distance between points A and B
g6-2024-045.why: The item plots a house and a school on a coordinate plane and asks for the distance plus the coordinates of both points and how they give the answer. Lesson 14's Cool-down is that task: given plotted points, state distances, and plot points from coordinates.

g6-2025-044.quote: What is the distance between points C and D?
g6-2025-044.why: The item asks for the distance from a cabbage patch at (5, -3) to a broccoli patch at (-2, -3) on a plotted coordinate plane, a horizontal span crossing the y-axis. Lesson 14's Cool-down asks for distances between plotted points in the same way; the axis-crossing case is developed in the same lesson's activity 'Finding Distances in a Coordinate Plane' (p. 176).

g6-2026-033.activity: Finding Distances in a Coordinate Plane
g6-2026-033.quote: Which of the points are 5 units from
g6-2026-033.why: The item gives four pairs of ordered pairs and asks which pair is 5 units apart, so students must test candidates rather than compute one distance. Lesson 14's second activity ends with the same inverted question, asking which of several points are 5 units from a given point.

g6-2023-021.quote: Find the perimeter of the polygon.
g6-2023-021.why: The item lists the four vertices of a quadrilateral with no picture and asks for the length of side AB, from (-4, 8) to (6, 8). Lesson 15's Cool-down has students plot a listed set of vertices, connect them into a polygon and find its perimeter, which requires computing exactly this kind of side length from coordinates.

g6-2024-037.quote: connect them in the order listed to create a polygon
g6-2024-037.why: The item shows a plotted parallelogram and asks the distance between vertices A (-6, 6) and D (4, 6). Lesson 15's Cool-down builds a polygon from listed vertices and asks for its perimeter, so every side length is computed from coordinates the way this item asks for one. Because the figure is supplied, Lesson 14's Cool-down 'Points and Distances' (p. 179) is an equally direct match for the arithmetic.

g6-2026-005.quote: Plot the following points in the coordinate plane, and connect them
g6-2026-005.why: The item lists the four vertices of a rectangle and asks for the length of side BC, from (4, 3) to (4, -7), a vertical side crossing the x-axis. Lesson 15's Cool-down asks students to plot listed vertices into a polygon and find its perimeter, which is the same work over every side.
